title: Risk Factors, Ultrasonographic-Histopathological Comparison, and Maternal Outcomes of the Placenta Accreta Spectrum: An Ambispective Cohort Study From a Tertiary Care Hospital in Northern India.
abstract: Aim Placenta accreta spectrum (PAS) is one of the leading causes of severe obstetric haemorrhage and peripartum hysterectomy, with a rising incidence due to increasing caesarean delivery rates worldwide. This study aimed to evaluate the risk factors for PAS, assess the concordance between ultrasonographic and histopathological findings, and determine maternal outcomes at a tertiary referral centre in northern India. Methods An ambispective observational study was conducted in the Department of Obstetrics and Gynaecology, Upper India Sugar Exchange Maternity Hospital, Ganesh Shankar Vidyarthi Memorial Medical College, Kanpur, India, between January 2020 and July 2024. Retrospective data (January 2020-December 2021) and prospective enrolment (January 2022-July 2024) were included in the study. Women with an antenatal or intraoperative diagnosis of PAS were included. Maternal demographics, obstetric history, intraoperative findings, transfusion requirements, intensive care admission, and maternal morbidity and mortality were recorded. Results Seventy women with PAS were identified during the 4.5-year study period. The institutional burden of PAS among women screened based on predefined risk factors increased from 20/720 (2.8%) in the retrospective period to 50/720 (6.9%) during the prospective period, with an overall burden of 70/1,440 (4.9%). Prior caesarean delivery was the dominant associated risk factor (62/70, 88.6%), with two prior caesarean deliveries in 28/70 cases (40.0%). Low-lying placenta was present in 20/70 women (28.6%), while placenta previa coexisted in 26/70 women (37.1%), giving a combined prevalence of 46/70 (65.7%). Caesarean hysterectomy was required in 58/70 women (82.85%), with a mean estimated blood loss of 1854.3 ± 417.3 mL and substantial perioperative transfusion requirements. One maternal death (1/70,1.43%) occurred; 9/70 (12.9%) women required intensive care. Histopathology confirmed all PAS cases (70/70,100%) and served as the reference standard. Ultrasonography correctly identified all cases of placenta increta (17/17, 100%) and placenta percreta (9/9, 100%) but detected only 26/44(59.1%) cases of placenta accreta. Conclusion Prior caesarean delivery and coexisting placenta previa were the principal risk factors in this cohort. The rising institutional burden of PAS highlighted the need for early antenatal diagnosis, structured referral pathways, and multidisciplinary perioperative care in tertiary centres.

title: Severe Dermatologic Toxicity During Amivantamab-Lazertinib Treatment in Epidermal Growth Factor Receptor (EGFR)-Mutated Non-Small Cell Lung Cancer.
abstract: Amivantamab is an epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) and mesenchymal-epithelial transition (MET) antibody. Lazertinib is an EGFR tyrosine kinase inhibitor with central nervous system penetration. Used in combination, this targeted therapy is effective in treating non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC). However, it has been associated with severe dermatologic adverse reactions. A 61-year-old woman with a history of EGFR-mutated NSCLC with brain metastases on amivantamab-lazertinib therapy presented for follow-up with drainage from her scalp incision after undergoing a right parietal craniotomy and mass excision five months prior. The patient denied constitutional and neurologic symptoms, but reported yellow staining on her pillow. Examination initially demonstrated yellow fibrinous exudate and hair matting along the surgical incision. Computed tomography (CT) of the head revealed overlying scalp swelling and minimal extra-axial dural thickening over the prior right parietal craniotomy site with stable intracranial metastatic lesions. Due to concern for dehiscence, her biologic therapy was paused, and she was taken to the operating suite where no evidence of infection, delayed healing, or wound dehiscence was noted. A 10 × 5 cm area of patchy granulation tissue and ulceration was observed along the right parietal scalp. Biopsy revealed granulation tissue and multinucleated giant cells and was negative for tumor. Given the risk of malignant progression with all targeted therapy paused, the patient was restarted on amivantamab monotherapy. Following disease progression two months later, she was transitioned to carboplatin and etoposide. EGFR is widely expressed in skin keratinocytes and intimately involved in epithelial differentiation. Therapies targeting EGFR, such as amivantamab plus lazertinib, are associated with adverse dermatologic reactions, ranging from dry skin to severe scalp ulceration, which can interrupt treatment, contribute to poorer clinical outcomes, and reduce quality of life. Standard of care includes limiting sun exposure and avoiding alcohol-based topical agents. The use of daily prophylactic antibiotics, such as oral doxycycline, topical clindamycin, chlorhexidine wash, and ceramide moisturizer, may significantly reduce the risk of adverse skin reactions. Implementation of this multicomponent regimen reduced the rate of severe scalp reactions from 26% to 10% relative to the standard of care, with sustained benefit observed for at least six months.

title: Prevalence of Endodontic-Periodontal Lesions and Associated Risk Factors Among Patients Undergoing Orthodontic Treatment: A Retrospective Observational Study.
abstract: Introduction Endodontic-periodontal (endo-perio) lesions are complex pathological conditions involving simultaneous pulpal and periodontal tissue destruction, posing considerable diagnostic and therapeutic challenges. Although orthodontic treatment may influence periodontal health, limited evidence exists regarding the prevalence of endo-perio lesions and their associated risk factors among orthodontic patients. This study aimed to determine the prevalence of endo-perio lesions among patients undergoing orthodontic treatment and to identify demographic, clinical, and radiographic factors associated with their occurrence. Materials and methods This retrospective observational study analyzed archived records of orthodontic patients. During the six-month record-review period, 1,250 orthodontic patient records were screened. Diagnosis was established using documented clinical findings, pulp vitality testing, and radiographic evaluation. Data were then analyzed, and continuous variables were compared using the independent-samples t test or Mann-Whitney U test, whereas categorical variables were compared using the chi-square test or Fisher's exact test. Independent predictors were identified using multivariable logistic regression. Statistical significance was established at p < 0.05. Results The overall prevalence of endo-perio lesions was 5.76% (72/1,250). Patients with lesions were significantly older than those without lesions (33.7 ± 9.8 vs. 28.1 ± 9.0 years; p < 0.001) and had a longer median orthodontic treatment duration (27.0 vs. 24.0 months; p = 0.009). Multivariable logistic regression identified that increasing age (adjusted OR = 1.04; 95% CI: 1.01-1.08; p = 0.012), molar teeth (adjusted OR = 2.87; 95% CI: 1.20-6.84; p = 0.017), non-vital pulp (adjusted OR = 52.90; 95% CI: 20.72-135.10; p < 0.001), deep periodontal pockets ≥5 mm (adjusted OR = 92.14; 95% CI: 21.80-389.50; p < 0.001), and radiographic bone loss (adjusted OR = 18.47; 95% CI: 5.46-62.52; p < 0.001) were independent predictors of endo-perio lesions. Conclusion Older age, molar teeth, non-vital pulp, deep periodontal pockets, and radiographic bone loss were significant independent predictors of lesion occurrence. Comprehensive periodontal examination, pulp vitality testing, and radiographic assessment should be routinely integrated into orthodontic care to facilitate early diagnosis and interdisciplinary management.

title: A Rare Coexistence of Arteria Lusoria, Truncus Bicaroticus, and Klippel-Feil Syndrome: A Five-Year Follow-Up and Procedural Considerations.
abstract: Arteria lusoria, an aberrant right subclavian artery (ARSA) arising as the most distal branch of the aortic arch, is the most common congenital aortic arch anomaly, yet it is clinically silent in over 90% of individuals and is usually discovered incidentally. We report the incidental identification of ARSA together with a truncus bicaroticus and Klippel-Feil syndrome (KFS) in a 32-year-old man investigated for intermittent pretracheal pressure. Contrast-enhanced MRI of the neck demonstrated a retro-oesophageal ARSA with mild oesophageal compression and revealed congenital fusion of the C2-C3 and C6-C7 vertebrae, consistent with KFS, together with suspected canal stenosis at C4-C5. Thoracic MR angiography confirmed ARSA with proximal ectasia at its origin, absence of a Kommerell's diverticulum (KD), and a truncus bicaroticus, alongside congenital right-sided latissimus dorsi and serratus anterior atrophy. Serial MR angiography over five years demonstrated no significant interval progression, and a conservative surveillance strategy was adopted in line with current guidelines. The coexistence of ARSA, truncus bicaroticus, and KFS in this patient raises the possibility of a shared developmental basis. Previously described embryological mechanisms, including the subclavian artery supply disruption sequence (SASDS), provide a plausible framework linking abnormalities of pharyngeal arch development and cervical somite segmentation during weeks 4-8 of gestation; however, such a relationship cannot be established from a single case. Beyond surveillance, the principal clinical message is procedural: unrecognised ARSA carries potentially avoidable risks during right transradial catheterisation, thyroid and anterior cervical surgery (through its association with a non-recurrent laryngeal nerve), and oesophageal, mediastinal, and thoracic procedures. Recognition of one component of this constellation may therefore warrant consideration of associated congenital anomalies and targeted vascular imaging, particularly when invasive cardiac, cervical, or thoracic procedures are planned.

title: Suprabasal Blistering as a Diagnostic Pitfall in Bullous Pemphigoid: Histopathologic-Immunofluorescence Discordance Complicated by Sepsis.
abstract: Bullous pemphigoid is the most common autoimmune subepidermal blistering disease, typically diagnosed through a combination of clinical features, histopathology, and direct immunofluorescence (DIF). However, histopathological findings can be misleading when re-epithelialization shifts the blister plane from subepidermal to suprabasal, mimicking pemphigus vulgaris. We present the case of a 58-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes mellitus, diabetic neuropathy, and a sacral pressure ulcer admitted with a three-week history of generalized tense bullae in a symmetric distribution across the trunk and extremities, with subsequent oral mucosal involvement. The disease was classified as severe bullous pemphigoid. Skin biopsy revealed a suprabasal blister with eosinophilic infiltrate, a pattern classically associated with pemphigus vulgaris; however, DIF demonstrated linear immunoglobulin G and complement C3c deposition at the dermoepidermal junction, confirming bullous pemphigoid and categorically ruling out pemphigus. Initial treatment with systemic corticosteroids and immunosuppressants was complicated by septic shock secondary to a catheter-related bloodstream infection, hospital-acquired pneumonia, and urinary tract infection, requiring vasopressor support, adjustment of the immunosuppressive regimen, and antimicrobial escalation. The patient also developed progressive multifactorial anemia, sepsis-associated coagulopathy, and upper gastrointestinal bleeding. Following multidisciplinary management, she achieved near-complete resolution of skin lesions and clinical recovery, and was discharged with plans for rituximab as definitive steroid-sparing therapy. This case highlights two critical lessons: first, a suprabasal blister on histopathology does not exclude bullous pemphigoid, as re-epithelialization can alter the apparent cleavage plane, making DIF indispensable for an accurate diagnosis; second, severe bullous pemphigoid requiring intensive immunosuppression carries a substantial risk of sequential nosocomial infections warranting close microbiological surveillance, early source control, and timely modulation of immunosuppressive regimens.

title: Recurrent Left Abducens Nerve Palsy and Idiopathic Intracranial Hypertension During Pregnancy: A Diagnostic Challenge.
abstract: Idiopathic intracranial hypertension (IIH) is characterized by elevated intracranial pressure without an identifiable mass lesion, hydrocephalus, cerebral venous sinus thrombosis, or abnormal cerebrospinal fluid composition. Diagnosis during pregnancy can be challenging because headache and visual symptoms overlap with several neurologic and obstetric disorders. We report a previously healthy 20-year-old primigravida with a body mass index of approximately 33 kg/m² who presented at 17 weeks' gestation with intermittent headache, photophobia, blurred vision, horizontal diplopia, nasal deviation of the left eye, and absent left-eye abduction. Visual acuity was 6/6 bilaterally, with mild bilateral optic disc swelling, greater on the left. The initial brain magnetic resonance imaging report described subtle paired diffusion-weighted signal abnormalities in the region of the medial longitudinal fasciculi, interpreted as possible mild cytotoxic edema related to a potentially reversible ischemic event. These findings were not anatomically concordant with the documented isolated left abduction deficit, and subsequent informal radiologic review raised the possibility that they were artifactual; no formal radiology addendum was available. Magnetic resonance angiography showed no significant intracranial arterial abnormality, and magnetic resonance venography excluded cerebral venous sinus thrombosis. Lumbar puncture in the lateral decubitus position demonstrated an opening pressure of 31 cmH₂O with normal cerebrospinal fluid constituents, followed by resolution of her symptoms and abducens palsy after drainage. Symptoms recurred at 20 weeks, when repeat opening pressure was 42 cmH₂O; and they again improved after drainage. Acetazolamide was commenced at 250 mg twice daily and increased to 500 mg twice daily at 33 weeks because of persistent optic disc swelling. The patient underwent cesarean delivery at 36 weeks; the specific clinical rationale for the mode of delivery was unavailable in the records reviewed. The neonate weighed 2.6 kg, had Apgar scores of seven and eight, and had no documented neonatal complications. Acetazolamide was continued postpartum. At telephone review approximately six months after delivery, the patient remained clinically well, reported adherence to her prescribed acetazolamide, and denied recurrent headache, blurred vision, diplopia, or ocular deviation. Final objective ophthalmologic resolution could not be confirmed because she did not attend her most recent scheduled ophthalmology follow-up. This case emphasizes the need to integrate clinical examination, cerebrospinal fluid findings, and neuroimaging when evaluating intracranial hypertension during pregnancy.

Symptoms recurred at 20 weeks, when repeat opening pressure was 42 cmH₂O; and they again improved after drainage. Acetazolamide was commenced at 250 mg twice daily and increased to 500 mg twice daily at 33 weeks because of persistent optic disc swelling. The patient underwent cesarean delivery at 36 weeks; the specific clinical rationale for the mode of delivery was unavailable in the records reviewed. The neonate weighed 2.6 kg, had Apgar scores of seven and eight, and had no documented neonatal complications. Acetazolamide was continued postpartum. At telephone review approximately six months after delivery, the patient remained clinically well, reported adherence to her prescribed acetazolamide, and denied recurrent headache, blurred vision, diplopia, or ocular deviation. Final objective ophthalmologic resolution could not be confirmed because she did not attend her most recent scheduled ophthalmology follow-up. This case emphasizes the need to integrate clinical examination, cerebrospinal fluid findings, and neuroimaging when evaluating intracranial hypertension during pregnancy.

title: Decades Later: Recurrent Gastrointestinal Sequelae in a Patient With Remote Metastatic Osteosarcoma to the Stomach and Colon.
abstract: Osteosarcoma is a primary malignant bone tumor with a well-established tendency for pulmonary metastasis; however, gastrointestinal (GI) involvement is exceedingly rare. Intra-abdominal metastases may occur years to decades after the initial diagnosis. Hematogenous spread, following pulmonary metastasis, is the presumed mechanism. Due to delayed presentation and atypical manifestations, recognition of GI complications in patients with a remote history of osteosarcoma is essential. In this report, we present a case of an 80-year-old male with chronic GI complications decades after original metastatic osteosarcoma diagnosis involving the stomach and colon. He described recurrent, dull, constant left lower quadrant abdominal pain associated with poor oral intake and constipation. Physical examination demonstrated focal left lower quadrant tenderness. CT abdomen and pelvis revealed dilated small bowel loops concerning for partial small bowel obstruction, while esophagram demonstrated esophageal dysmotility with mild reflux. These findings are linked to the sequelae of complications following initial metastatic osteosarcoma. The patient had a history of numerous surgeries and required continuous opioid use for pain management. Conservative management consisted of bowel rest, laxatives, and supportive care resulting in transient symptom improvement; however, symptoms recurred frequently following discharge, leading to multiple readmissions for recurrent obstructive and dysmotility-related symptoms. This case highlights several gastroenterological considerations. Metastatic osteosarcoma and further GI sequelae should remain within the differential diagnoses of chronic abdominal pain or bowel obstruction in patients with a remote history of osteosarcoma, even decades after initial treatment. For gastroenterologists, recognition of both structural and functional GI sequelae of osteosarcoma is critical to guide symptom-directed, nonoperative management strategies and reduce recurrent hospitalizations.

title: Breast Metastasis From Cervical Small Cell Neuroendocrine Carcinoma Mimicking Primary Breast Cancer.
abstract: We describe a case of breast metastasis originating from a small-cell neuroendocrine carcinoma (SCNEC) of the uterine cervix, an uncommon presentation that can be difficult to distinguish from a primary breast malignancy. We report a 29-year-old woman treated three years earlier for FIGO stage IB2 cervical SCNEC with chemotherapy, surgery, and radiotherapy, who presented with a 1.5-cm mass in the left breast. Imaging suggested a primary breast malignancy, but her oncologic history raised concern for metastasis. Core-needle biopsy showed a high-grade small-cell neoplasm expressing synaptophysin, chromogranin A, and CD56, with a high Ki-67 index (>80%); breast-lineage markers, including GATA3 and mammaglobin, were negative. Whole-body fluorodeoxyglucose positron emission tomography-computed tomography (FDG PET-CT) showed an isolated hypermetabolic breast lesion without other disease. Nipple-sparing mastectomy with immediate reconstruction was performed, followed by platinum-etoposide chemotherapy; at 18 months, there was no evidence of recurrence. Breast metastasis from cervical SCNEC can mimic primary breast cancer; diagnosis relies on integrating clinical history, imaging, and immunohistochemistry. Selected patients with isolated disease may benefit from individualised multimodal therapy.

title: Boerhaave Syndrome Caused by Pancreatitis-Induced Gastric Outlet Obstruction: A Case Report.
abstract: Boerhaave syndrome is a spontaneous transmural perforation of the esophagus, typically triggered by forceful vomiting and carrying a high mortality rate when diagnosis is delayed. We present a 56-year-old man with chronic alcohol use disorder who developed esophageal perforation through an unusual causal chain. He presented with intractable vomiting, hematemesis, and cervical subcutaneous emphysema. Computed tomography showed posterior pneumomediastinum and marked gastric and duodenal distention caused by an inflammatory cephalopancreatic mass. Elevated pancreatic enzymes confirmed acute pancreatitis. The sequence appeared to be alcoholic pancreatitis compressing the duodenum, causing gastric outlet obstruction, protracted emesis, and esophageal rupture. On the day of admission, laparoscopic primary two-layer esophagorrhaphy and gastrojejunostomy were performed to address both the perforation and the duodenal obstruction. The postoperative course was complicated by recurrent pancreatitis and bilateral pleural effusions, but serial imaging confirmed no leak at the esophageal repair or the anastomosis. The patient was discharged on postoperative day 25. Follow-up magnetic resonance cholangiopancreatography excluded pancreatic malignancy and showed findings consistent with groove pancreatitis and chronic pancreatitis. This case illustrates an unusual causal chain in which acute pancreatitis led to esophageal perforation via gastric outlet obstruction and reinforces the benefit of same-day surgical repair when both the perforation and its cause can be addressed in a single procedure.

title: Chronic Ulnar-Sided Wrist Pain Caused by a Rare Glomangioma: A Case Report.
abstract: Glomus tumors are benign neoplasms typically found in the fingers and usually present with localized pain, swelling, and cold sensitivity. Extradigital glomus tumors are rare, and their diagnosis is often delayed due to atypical location and lack of cold sensitivity. In this article, we report a unique case of an extradigital glomangioma, a subset of glomus tumors, masquerading as more common ulnar-sided wrist pathology, such as a triangular fibrocartilage complex tear or extensor carpi ulnaris tendinitis. The patient presented with a two-year history of gradually worsening ulnar-sided wrist pain with no history of trauma. Examination revealed localized tenderness on the ulnar wrist without a palpable mass. X-rays were normal, and the pain was unresponsive to nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory medication and cortisone injection. Magnetic resonance imaging revealed a subcentimeter mass in the subcutaneous fat on the ulnar side of the wrist. The lesion was bright on T2-weighted and IV gadolinium-enhanced sequences. Excisional biopsy allowed the pathological diagnosis of benign glomangioma to be established. The patient reported immediate, complete resolution of pain postoperatively. This case underscores the importance of advanced imaging, clinical vigilance, and surgical excision for this rare tumor.

title: Acinetobacter baumannii Nosocomial Meningitis Secondary to Neurosurgical Intervention: A Case Report.
abstract: Nosocomial meningitis is a serious complication of neurosurgical procedures, associated with high morbidity and mortality, as well as significant diagnostic and therapeutic challenges. Among the causative pathogens, Acinetobacter baumannii (A. baumannii) is particularly concerning due to its ability to survive for prolonged periods in the hospital environment, its opportunistic virulence, and, especially, its tendency to develop multidrug resistance to antimicrobial agents. Diagnosis is often difficult in the postoperative setting, particularly when the cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) is altered as a result of the surgical procedure. Rapid identification of the causative agent and early initiation of appropriate antibiotic therapy are essential to limit complications and improve patient prognosis. We report the case of a 27-year-old patient with a history of surgically treated craniopharyngioma complicated by anterior hypopituitarism. Three weeks after surgery, he was admitted to the ICU with suspected postoperative meningitis due to the onset of behavioral disturbances associated with nasal discharge, without a fever. Brain CT was normal. CSF analysis, obtained by lumbar puncture under strict aseptic conditions, revealed a turbid fluid with leukocytosis of 5,760 cells/mm³, predominantly composed of neutrophils, along with elevated protein levels (5.7 g/L) and low glucose levels (0.05 g/L). Direct examination after Gram staining showed Gram-negative coccobacilli with a marked inflammatory reaction. CSF culture grew a multidrug-resistant (MDR) strain of A. baumannii , which was sensitive only to colistin. The patient received antibiotic therapy with colistin, administered intravenously and intrathecally for 18 days, with initial neurological improvement and sterilization of the CSF by the 15th day of treatment. The subsequent course was unfavorable, marked by the development of acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS) secondary to ventilator-associated pneumonia caused by methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA), complicated by refractory septic shock, which ultimately led to his death after one month of hospitalization in the ICU. This report highlights the severity of nosocomial meningitis caused by MDR A. baumannii and underscores the importance of implementing infection prevention measures in healthcare settings.

title: The Hidden Hitchhiker: Retrocaval Ureter Masquerading as Isolated Pelviureteric Junction Obstruction.
abstract: The coexistence of true pelviureteric junction obstruction (PUJO) and a retrocaval ureter in a single, non-duplicated collecting system is exceptionally rare, and this case represents a "hidden retrocaval ureter," in which an upstream PUJO masked the classical radiological features, transforming the diagnosis into an unexpected intraoperative discovery. Our case highlights such a peculiar case, where a 70-year-old man with longstanding intermittent right loin pain was found to have right hydronephrosis and a serum creatinine of 1.7 mg/dL. Computed tomography showed a markedly dilated extra-renal pelvis resembling PUJO. The radiological report suggested a ureteric stricture at that level. Magnetic resonance urography also showed an abrupt medial narrowing at the L3-L4 level, but the ureter could not be seen passing behind the inferior vena cava (IVC). The abrupt medial kink raised suspicion of a retrocaval ureter. During robotic surgery, the ureter was found coursing behind the IVC, confirming a retrocaval ureter. Surprisingly, dividing this segment did not decompress the tense renal pelvis. Further dissection revealed a separate narrowing at the true PUJ, and urine was released only after the pelvis was opened above this obstruction. The PUJO had prevented urine from entering the retrocaval segment, which explained why it was not visible on preoperative imaging. Both narrowed segments were excised, the ureter was brought anterior to the IVC, and pyeloureteral reconstruction was performed over a double-J stent. This case is unusual not only because the two conditions occurred together but also because one obstruction concealed the other.

title: Patient-Reported Barriers to Mammography Screening Among Women at a Community Health Clinic in Southeastern Michigan: A Cross-Sectional Pilot Study.
abstract: Background The objective of this cross-sectional pilot study was to explore patient-reported barriers to mammography screening and women's knowledge, attitudes, and behaviors regarding mammography among women receiving care at a university-affiliated community health clinic in Southeastern Michigan (SEM). Methods A 47-item investigator-developed exploratory questionnaire informed by the Health Belief Model (HBM) constructs was distributed via Qualtrics from August to December 2025 to women receiving care at a local community health clinic. The questionnaire assessed the participants' awareness, perceptions, attitudes, and comfort regarding mammogram screening. Descriptive statistics were calculated for completed questionnaires, and patient-reported barriers were categorized using prespecified response categories. Results Twenty-one adult women aged 18 and older completed the questionnaire. Findings demonstrated that most participants were unaware of affordable or free mammogram services (81%, n = 17), while 28.6% (n = 6) reported language as a barrier in healthcare. The perception of mammography costs also varied across insurance groups. Conclusion This community-focused pilot study provides preliminary insights into the perceptions, beliefs, attitudes, experiences, and potential barriers related to mammography screenings among women receiving care at a community health clinic in SEM. Although these preliminary findings should be interpreted with caution due to their exploratory study design and small convenience sample, they may inform future community-oriented research examining barriers to mammography screening and the development of region-specific educational and outreach strategies.

title: Bilateral Maxillary Fourth and Fifth Molars in a 17-Year-Old Female.
abstract: Supernumerary teeth are relatively common in clinical practice; however, the occurrence of multiple supernumerary teeth in a bilaterally symmetrical pattern is rare. A 17-year-old female was referred to our department for extraction of impacted third molars. Panoramic radiography revealed two bilaterally symmetrical tooth-like structures adjacent to each maxillary third molar. Computed tomography confirmed that these were independent structures, leading to a diagnosis of bilateral maxillary fourth and fifth molars. In July 2023, the bilateral maxillary and mandibular third molars, together with the bilateral maxillary fourth and fifth molars, were extracted under general anesthesia. Gross examination of the extracted teeth revealed morphological features consistent with molar teeth. This case highlights the importance of accurate three-dimensional imaging and individualized treatment strategies in the management of complex and rare presentations of supernumerary teeth.

title: When Tuberculosis Left the Heart in a Cage: Multimodality Imaging Revealing Constrictive Pericarditis in a Young Adult.
abstract: Tuberculous pericarditis (TBP) is a potentially severe manifestation of extrapulmonary tuberculosis that may lead to pericardial effusion and constrictive physiology and, in some patients, progress to fixed constrictive pericarditis. Diagnosis can be particularly challenging in young immunocompetent patients without overt pulmonary involvement. We report the case of a 20-year-old immunocompetent man presenting with a one-month history of weight loss, profuse night sweats, nocturnal fever, and typical pericarditic chest pain. Clinical examination revealed fever and signs of systemic venous congestion. Transthoracic echocardiography demonstrated marked pericardial thickening, moderate circumferential effusion, septal bounce, approximately 25% respiratory variation in transmitral flow, annulus reversus, and annulus paradoxus, supporting the presence of pericardial effusion with constrictive physiology. Contrast-enhanced computed tomography confirmed diffuse pericardial thickening and effusion without calcification or pulmonary parenchymal involvement. At the same time, cardiac magnetic resonance demonstrated intense late gadolinium enhancement of the thickened pericardium, supporting active pericardial inflammation. Xpert Mycobacterium tuberculosis/Rifampicin assay (Xpert MTB/RIF; Cepheid, Sunnyvale, CA, USA) testing of the pericardial fluid detected Mycobacterium tuberculosis, subsequently confirmed by positive mycobacterial culture. Following multidisciplinary discussion, a six-month antituberculous regimen combined with adjunctive corticosteroid therapy was initiated, with close clinical and multimodality imaging follow-up and reassessment for pericardiectomy according to clinical evolution. This case highlights the complementary value of echocardiography, computed tomography, and cardiac magnetic resonance in characterizing tuberculous pericardial disease associated with constrictive physiology and defining its inflammatory substrate. Identification of active pericardial inflammation in the presence of constrictive physiology may indicate a potentially reversible component; however, actual reversibility requires confirmation during longer-term follow-up.

title: Intraoperative Challenges of Patient-Specific Osteotomy Guides in Anterior Maxillary Osteotomy: A Case Report.
abstract: Orthognathic surgery has increasingly incorporated digital workflows and patient-specific surgical guides to enhance accuracy and predictability. While these technologies offer improved planning and execution, their intraoperative application in segmented maxillary osteotomies remains technically demanding. Limited literature exists describing the practical challenges encountered during guide-assisted osteotomy, particularly in anatomically constrained regions. This case report describes the use of a patient-specific cutting guide in a 24-year-old male patient undergoing anterior two-piece maxillary osteotomy for correction of skeletal Class II malocclusion with gummy smile. Virtual surgical planning was performed using cone-beam computed tomography and digital dental models to simulate a 7 mm maxillary setback and 4 mm superior impaction. A custom osteotomy guide and surgical splint were fabricated using computer-aided design (CAD)/computer-aided manufacturing (CAM) technology. Intraoperatively, the guide was positioned following mucoperiosteal flap elevation and used to perform vertical and horizontal osteotomy cuts. The maxillary segment was mobilized, repositioned using a prefabricated occlusal splint, and stabilized with titanium miniplates. The use of the osteotomy guide facilitated accurate transfer of the planned osteotomy lines and segment repositioning. However, intraoperative challenges were encountered, including increased operative time due to guide positioning and verification, limited access during osteotomy cuts, and difficulty in executing palatal osteotomy. Initial instability of the guide due to soft tissue interference required intraoperative adjustment. A minor palatal mucosal tear occurred, which was managed conservatively. Despite these challenges, satisfactory occlusal alignment and postoperative stability were achieved.

title: Malignant Posterior Reversible Encephalopathy Syndrome (PRES) After Allogeneic Hematopoietic Stem Cell Transplantation Requiring Emergency Decompressive Craniectomy: A Case Report.
abstract: Posterior reversible encephalopathy syndrome (PRES) is a neurological disorder characterized by nonspecific acute neurological signs and symptoms combined with typical imaging findings. It usually has a favorable prognosis but can occasionally be complicated by severe and life-threatening manifestations. Malignant PRES is the most severe form of this condition, defined by coma, refractory intracranial hypertension, and radiological evidence of cerebral edema or hemorrhage associated with a mass effect. We report a case of a 53-year-old woman with high-risk myelodysplastic neoplasm with increased blasts-2 who underwent allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplantation. The post-allograft period was complicated by grade III acute graft-versus-host disease, which required intensified immunosuppression with high-dose prednisolone and therapeutic doses of cyclosporine. Eighty-three days after transplantation, the patient was admitted to the emergency department with acute neurological symptoms. Rapid development of coma and clinical signs of intracranial hypertension, refractory to osmotic therapy with mannitol and hypertonic saline, prompted an emergency decompressive craniectomy. Magnetic resonance imaging confirmed the diagnosis of malignant PRES. Withdrawal of cyclosporine, mycophenolate mofetil, and voriconazole, along with intensive supportive management in the neurocritical care unit, resulted in complete neurological recovery.

title: Diagnostic Performance of ACR TI-RADS, EU-TI-RADS, and Individual Ultrasound Features for Predicting Thyroid Malignancy: A Histopathology-Validated Analysis of Surgically Excised Nodules.
abstract: The primary objective was to compare the histopathology-validated diagnostic performance of the American College of Radiology Thyroid Imaging Reporting and Data System (ACR TI-RADS) and the European Thyroid Imaging Reporting and Data System (EU-TI-RADS) for predicting malignancy in surgically excised thyroid nodules. Secondary objectives were to evaluate the discriminatory contribution of individual ultrasound features, characterize threshold-specific classification errors, examine performance by malignant histological subtype, and assess the potential influence of within-patient clustering. In this retrospective secondary analysis of an institutional review board-approved cohort, 284 surgically excised thyroid nodules from 233 patients (170 female, 73.0%; mean age: 43.5 ± 10.9 years) were analysed using postoperative histopathology as the reference standard. Nodules were categorized using ACR TI-RADS and EU-TI-RADS. Diagnostic performance was assessed using receiver operating characteristic (ROC) analysis and threshold-based 2×2 contingency tables. Sensitivity, specificity, accuracy, positive predictive value (PPV), and negative predictive value (NPV) were reported as n/N (%), with 95% confidence intervals. Confusion matrix analysis was performed to evaluate true-positive, false-positive, true-negative, and false-negative classifications. Because some patients contributed more than one nodule, the potential influence of within-patient clustering was evaluated using cluster-size characterization and a single-index-nodule sensitivity analysis. Multivariable regression modelling and formal interobserver agreement analysis were not performed and are addressed in the Limitations section. Histopathology identified 150/284 malignant nodules (52.8%) and 134/284 benign nodules (47.2%). ACR TI-RADS showed the highest discriminatory performance (AUC of 0.950 for point score and 0.948 for categories), followed by EU-TI-RADS (AUC of 0.933). At clinically relevant thresholds, ACR TI-RADS TR4 or higher identified 131/150 malignant nodules and correctly classified 127/134 benign nodules, yielding sensitivity 87.3%, specificity 94.8%, and accuracy 90.8%. EU-TI-RADS category 4 or higher identified 130/150 malignant nodules and correctly classified 130/134 benign nodules, yielding a sensitivity of 86.7%, a specificity of 97.0%, and an accuracy of 91.5%. ACR TI-RADS produced slightly fewer false-negative classifications, whereas EU-TI-RADS produced fewer false-positive classifications. ACR TI-RADS and EU-TI-RADS both demonstrated excellent histopathology-validated diagnostic performance in this surgically enriched cohort. Differences between the systems mainly reflected distinct classification error profiles rather than clear superiority of one system. Feature-level and confusion matrix analyses provided additional clinically relevant information, but the findings should be interpreted in the context of surgical-selection bias and may not be directly generalizable to unselected thyroid nodule populations. Because this was a surgically enriched cohort with a malignancy prevalence of 52.8%, predictive values should not be extrapolated to unselected screening or surveillance populations. Sensitivity, specificity, and AUC may also differ in unselected populations because of spectrum and verification bias. Prospective multicenter validation is required.

title: Diabetes Insipidus as a Rare Complication of Metastatic Breast Cancer With Pituitary Metastases.
abstract: Diabetes insipidus (DI) is a rare but significant and life-threatening complication of metastatic breast cancer, typically arising when cancer spreads to the pituitary gland. This condition results from impaired secretion or action of antidiuretic hormone (ADH) or arginine vasopressin (AVP), leading to symptoms including excessive urination and thirst. The posterior lobe of the pituitary and the infundibulum are most susceptible to metastatic involvement due to their direct arterial blood supply, making them more accessible to circulating tumor cells. This phenomenon explains why DI can be a manifestation of pituitary metastases. We report the case of a patient who presented with a five-week history of projectile vomiting, dizziness, blurred vision, headache, insatiable thirst, and nocturia. She reported urinating up to 12 times at night such that she struggled to sleep and would end up having daytime lethargy and fatigue. Biochemical evaluation demonstrated hyperosmolar serum, low urine osmolality, and low urine sodium, consistent with central DI. MRI revealed a pituitary stalk and suprasellar metastases with multiple new cerebral and cerebellar lesions. The patient underwent a desmopressin challenge leading to rapid improvement in polyuria and an increase in urine osmolality. Desmopressin confirmed an intact renal response, establishing the diagnosis of cranial DI secondary to pituitary metastases. Despite symptomatic benefit, her overall condition deteriorated due to progressive intracranial and systemic disease. She subsequently received whole-brain radiotherapy and palliative care but died three months after the diagnosis of DI. This case highlights central DI as a rare but clinically important manifestation of pituitary metastases in metastatic breast cancer. Prompt recognition and endocrine replacement, particularly with desmopressin, can provide meaningful symptomatic relief even when prognosis remains poor. Early multidisciplinary involvement, including endocrinology, oncology, radiology, and palliative care, is essential for optimizing quality of life in such complex cases.

title: Mimicking Polycystic Liver Disease: A Case Report of Innumerable Cystic Hepatic Metastases From a Pancreatic Neuroendocrine Tumour and Diagnostic Role of Endoscopic Ultrasound.
abstract: Pancreatic neuroendocrine tumours (PNETs) are malignant processes and are identified as being the rarest of all pancreatic cancers. Here we present the case of a 62-year-old male with a background of chronic lymphocytic leukaemia (CLL) who was investigated over 18 months for progressive hepatic cystic lesions with no known aetiology. Imaging revealed main pancreatic duct dilatation without an identifiable intrinsic or extrinsic cause, coupled with enlarged mesenteric lymph nodes. Endoscopic ultrasound identified multiple cystic liver lesions of different sizes, some reflecting the presence of septations. The calibre of the main pancreatic duct was noted to be dilated in the absence of calculi, raising suspicion for a focal inflammatory process or chronic pancreatitis. Fine needle aspiration was performed from the pancreas, liver and lymph nodes; samples were sent for cytological analysis. This revealed the presence of a well-differentiated neuroendocrine tumour, WHO grade 2, across all three sites. The neuroendocrine multidisciplinary team (MDT) classified the tumor as stage T1N1M1a and recommended treatment with somatostatin analogue with palliative intent. This case reflects the diagnostic challenges of atypical PNET presentations and emphasises the crucial role of endoscopic ultrasound with tissue sampling in establishing a definitive diagnosis.

title: Understanding CT Resolution Timeline in Acute Pyelonephritis: A Framework for Clinical Practice.
abstract: Background Acute pyelonephritis is diagnosed based on clinical and laboratory signs. Computed tomography (CT) is typically reserved for detecting complications or alternative diagnoses. Current guidelines do not recommend routine follow-up imaging when abnormalities are found. The expected time to resolution (TTR) of CT abnormalities has not been clearly identified, which serves as the goal of our study. Methodology This retrospective study was conducted at an academic hospital in Harris County, Texas. Adult patients with a diagnosis of acute pyelonephritis who underwent at least two CT scans were included. Three board-certified radiologists independently reviewed CT studies performed within one year of the index scan and assessed for striated nephrogram, parenchymal edema, patchy hypodensities, perinephric fat stranding, and urothelial thickening. Time to first documented radiologic resolution (TTR) was defined as the interval between the first positive CT sign and the first subsequent CT in which the sign was absent. TTR was calculated for individual signs and globally, provided clinical criteria for pyelonephritis were met. Sensitivity, specificity, and inter-rater agreement were also evaluated. Results A total of 288 CT scans from 93 patients were reviewed, of which 252 (88%) were of sufficient quality for analysis. The mean global TTR was 149 ± 100 days, with wide variation across individual signs. Moreover, imaging abnormalities persisted for 105 days despite clinical resolution. Conclusions CT signs consistent with pyelonephritis may persist for several months after clinical recovery. Clinicians should interpret persistent imaging abnormalities appropriately to avoid unnecessary diagnostic or therapeutic interventions.

title: Glioblastoma Masquerading as a Presumed Ischemic Stroke: A Case of Delusional Jealousy and Fluctuating Psychosis.
abstract: Psychiatric symptoms can be the presenting or dominant manifestation of an underlying brain tumor, and this phenomenon is frequently misattributed to a primary psychiatric disorder, particularly when a plausible alternative explanation, such as a recent stroke or a known alcohol use disorder, is already present. We report a case in which glioblastoma was ultimately identified as the cause of a subacute psychotic syndrome that had initially been attributed to a preceding cerebrovascular diagnosis. A 64-year-old man with a history of alcohol use disorder was admitted to Internal Medicine with a diagnosis of ischemic stroke in the left middle cerebral artery territory, with new-onset seizures at admission and a self-limited episode of hyperactive delirium. Four days after discharge, he was brought to a psychiatric emergency service with heteroaggression toward his wife, near-total insomnia, pressured speech, and delusions of infidelity and persecution. A head computed tomography scan and initial laboratory workup, including toxicology, were unremarkable, and he was admitted to Psychiatry with a presumptive diagnosis of new-onset psychotic disorder. Over 14 days, despite escalating antipsychotic therapy, he developed progressively incoherent speech, disorientation, and a fluctuating level of consciousness alternating between agitation and obnubilation. Family interviews clarified that his premorbid jealousy had been alcohol-related and transient, unlike the fixed, treatment-refractory delusion now present, and that confusion and fluctuating consciousness were new since the stroke admission. Magnetic resonance imaging revealed an infiltrative left temporo-insular and basal ganglia lesion radiologically consistent with glioblastoma, later confirmed histologically as an isocitrate dehydrogenase-wildtype, grade 4 tumor. The patient underwent subtotal resection; treatment was later limited to palliative care because of tumor progression, and he died five months afterward. This case illustrates that fluctuating consciousness, disorientation, and treatment-refractory psychosis in a patient with a recent stroke or seizure disorder should prompt reconsideration of the working diagnosis and contrast-enhanced magnetic resonance imaging, since a normal computed tomography scan does not exclude an infiltrating glioma, and neighboring organic syndromes can mimic one another both clinically and radiologically.

title: Correlation of the Diagnostic Accuracy of Dual Energy Computed Tomography and Positron Emission Tomography/Computed Tomography in Mediastinal Lymph Node Staging in Lung Cancer: A Systematic Review.
abstract: This study aims to correlate the accuracy of derived parameters of dual-energy computed tomography (DECT) against the reference imaging modality of choice, positron-emission tomography/computed tomography (PET/CT), in the diagnosis and staging of mediastinal lymph nodes in lung cancer. An extensive database search was conducted to retrieve literature comparing the performance of DECT parameters against PET/CT. Articles published between 2010 and January 2025 were retrieved from Embase, Web of Science, PubMed/MEDLINE (Medical Literature Analysis and Retrieval System Online), CINAHL (Cumulative Index to Nursing and Allied Health Literature), and Ovid. Articles were screened and selected based on clearly defined inclusion criteria. Methodological quality, heterogeneity, and bias were evaluated, and data were extracted and synthesized to identify correlations between DECT parameters and PET/CT parameters in mediastinal lymph node staging. Five articles that met the inclusion criteria were included in this review; these consisted of 212 patients, with 314 pathological mediastinal lymph nodes. DECT attenuation parameters including arterial phase/delayed phase ratio (A/D ratio) or maximum iodine related attenuation (IRAmax) were either strongly or moderately correlated with maximum standard uptake value (SUVmax) in PET/CT (r=0.80, p =0.027; r = 0.57, p= 0.047), and iodine concentration or iodine density had a weak or no correlation with SUVmax (r=0.23, p=0.14; r=0.064, p =0.453). 18fluorine-fluorodeoxyglucose (18F-FDG) PET/CT is the imaging modality of choice in the diagnosis of suspected mediastinal lymph nodes, but it is not widely accessible and has higher cost and high false positive rates. This review investigated the potential role of DECT as a possible surrogate of 18F-FDG PET/CT and found a good correlation between DECT attenuation parameters (only) and SUVmax in 18F-FDG PET/CT. There is a significant gap in the literature in relation to the investigation of this correlation. This review found that in DECT, attenuation parameters either strongly or moderately correlated with SUVmax from 18F-FDG PET/CT and may serve as an excellent complement; however, it may be inadequate to replace 18F-FDG-PET/CT in mediastinal lymph node staging in lung cancer.

title: Isolated Aphasia as an Epileptic Manifestation of Neurosarcoidosis: A Case Report.
abstract: Acute aphasia requires urgent evaluation for stroke, but recurrent and stereotyped language disturbances may also reflect focal seizures. We report the case of a 23-year-old man brought to the emergency department (ED) with aphasia that had been present for approximately six hours. Over the preceding week, he had experienced several similar but briefer episodes that had resolved spontaneously. He was concurrently undergoing investigation at another institution for persistent hiccups and near-daily vomiting of more than one month's duration. Chest computed tomography (CT) and positron emission tomography (PET)-computed tomography had already shown mediastinal and mesenteric lymphadenopathy suggestive of sarcoidosis, although other etiologies, including malignancy, could not be excluded. Neurological examination was limited by the language disturbance but showed no obvious motor deficit. Brain computed tomography revealed obstructive hydrocephalus with transependymal cerebrospinal fluid flow and multiple enhancing nodular lesions, predominantly in and around the ventricular system. Electroencephalography demonstrated epileptiform activity, and the aphasia resolved after treatment with levetiracetam and clobazam. Further cerebrospinal fluid analysis, magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), and pathological investigations supported a diagnosis of probable neurosarcoidosis presenting with lymphocytic meningoencephalitis and obstructive hydrocephalus. This case illustrates an unusual pathophysiological sequence, isolated aphasia as a focal epileptic manifestation of neurosarcoidosis, and is a reminder that unexplained focal neurological symptoms, particularly when fluctuating or recurrent, warrant the consideration of seizures and early electroencephalography.

title: Thoracotomy for Urgent Repair of Lung Torsion Identified as an Incidental Finding.
abstract: We report a 68-year-old male with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease on home oxygen who presented with foot swelling and erythema, associated with a new right foot wound. He denied chest pain and overt shortness of breath at the time of his presentation. Initial chest radiography obtained during the evaluation raised concern for pneumothorax versus a large bulla. Computed tomography with intravenous contrast and computed tomography angiography revealed an expanding right lower lobe bulla extending into the upper lung zone, narrowing of the right bronchial tree, and abnormal right hilar vasculature orientation concerning for lung torsion. Bronchoscopy demonstrated compression of the right upper lobe bronchus and severe compression of the right middle and lower lobe bronchi. The right lower and middle lobes were detorsed, and the bullous right lower lobe tissue was removed by wedge resection. Test inflation demonstrated satisfactory expansion, and there were no intraoperative complications. The postoperative course was complicated by a pleural effusion requiring decortication two weeks postoperatively, after which the patient recovered well. This case highlights how lung torsion may be identified incidentally and require urgent operative repair despite an inconspicuous respiratory presentation.

title: Sustained Regression of Parotid Mucosa-Associated Lymphoid Tissue (MALT) Lymphoma After Nutritional and Nutraceutical Intervention Without Chemoimmunotherapy: A Case Report.
abstract: Extranodal marginal zone lymphoma of mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue (MALT) in the setting of Sjögren's syndrome (SS) is a well-recognized complication of chronic autoimmune salivary gland inflammation. Standard management options include radiotherapy, immunotherapy, and combination chemoimmunotherapy, with active surveillance reserved for stable, low-burden disease. The potential role of structured nutritional and nutraceutical intervention in this setting has not been previously described. We report the case of a woman who presented at age 52 with SS-associated bilateral parotid MALT lymphoma that progressed substantially over 28 months of active observation, with palpable bilateral parotid enlargement reaching 10 x 5 cm on the left and 6 x 6 cm on the right. Proposed chemoimmunotherapy was deferred by the patient, and she independently initiated a structured multicomponent protocol comprising a strict vegan diet restricted in methionine and cysteine, urinary alkalization, and orally administered nutraceuticals including therapeutic-dose slow-releasing sodium selenite (32 mg/day), B6 pyridoxal-5'-phosphate (P5P), iron, zinc, copper, and manganese, with adjunctive rectal ozone therapy started at approximately Month 3. Serial clinical examinations and ultrasonography documented progressive bilateral parotid regression from approximately Month 7. At Month 20, repeat ultrasonography confirmed substantial radiographic reduction: the right parotid lesion decreased to 1.5 × 0.8 cm and the left to 2.7 × 0.8 cm, with both parotid glands returning to normal overall size with residual hypoechoic lesions and no cervical lymphadenopathy. At approximately Month 19, the hematologist documented no significant lymphadenopathy or splenomegaly on serial physical examination. Prednisone dosing, prescribed for concurrent autoimmune hemolytic anemia (AIHA), fluctuated independently of parotid gland changes throughout, making a corticosteroid-mediated response unlikely. This case documents a rapid and durable regression of progressive bilateral parotid MALT lymphoma after a dietary and nutraceutical protocol targeting tumor redox biology, without chemoimmunotherapy. Although spontaneous regression cannot be excluded, the response timing and proposed mechanism of glutathione and thioredoxin antioxidant pathway disruption merit further clinical study.

title: Vocal Fold Granuloma Causing Acute Airway Obstruction in a Pediatric Patient.
abstract: Vocal fold granuloma (VFG) is a benign laryngeal lesion caused by mucosal trauma to the arytenoid cartilage. Pediatric VFG is rare and is most often associated with prolonged or traumatic intubation. We present the case of a seven-year-old male who developed a 1-cm pedunculated VFG following two separate brief intubations for minor procedures. The lesion produced a dynamic "ball-valve" effect, resulting in biphasic stridor, breathy dysphonia, and intermittent airway obstruction. While computed tomography (CT) imaging was inconclusive, laryngoscopy identified a pedunculated lesion prolapsing into the subglottis with near-complete intermittent glottic obstruction. The mass was successfully excised, and the patient was extubated after a short course of intravenous steroids with complete resolution of symptoms. This case emphasizes that VFG should remain in the differential diagnosis for pediatric patients presenting with stridor and airway compromise following even brief periods of intubation.

title: Cerebral Aspergillosis in a Patient on Ibrutinib: A Case of Diagnostic Ambiguity and Multidisciplinary Care.
abstract: This case report describes the challenging diagnosis and management of cerebral aspergillosis in a patient with chronic lymphocytic leukaemia undergoing treatment with a BTK inhibitor. The initial presentation was deceptively unspecific, comprising cognitive changes, receptive aphasia, gait instability and mild neurological deficits without fever or significant systemic inflammation. The combination of a muted and non-indicative clinical picture and a broad differential diagnosis reflects the evolving complexity of CNS infections in patients treated with targeted haematological therapies. Neuroimaging played a central role in directing attention toward an intracranial pathological process but did not resolve the ambiguity. CT suggested a space-occupying lesion, while MRI revealed multiple enhancing foci with mixed signal characteristics that could represent fungal, bacterial or neoplastic processes. Diagnosis was only established after neurosurgical intervention, when resection of the dominant lesion provided tissue for definitive identification of Aspergillus fumigatus. Once the diagnosis was confirmed, long-term voriconazole therapy was initiated and adjusted with therapeutic drug monitoring, while ibrutinib was discontinued to prevent interactions and further immunosuppression. The patient's clinical trajectory gradually stabilised, with radiological follow-up showing resolution of lesions and no recurrence. Overall, this case illustrates the importance of maintaining a high index of suspicion for fungal CNS infections in patients receiving modern immunomodulatory treatments. The interplay between subtle and non-specific neurological clinical signs, atypical imaging and altered immune responses can delay diagnosis unless the clinical team actively integrates therapeutic background and invasive modalities into its reasoning. The favourable outcome achieved here underscores the value of early multidisciplinary involvement, timely pursuit of tissue diagnosis and careful coordination of antifungal therapy.

title: Factors Associated With 30-Day Functional Outcome and Mortality Following Spontaneous Intracerebral Hemorrhage in Bangladesh: A Prospective Two-Center Cohort Study.
abstract: Background Spontaneous intracerebral hemorrhage remains a major cause of early mortality and disability worldwide, with a disproportionate burden in low- and middle-income countries such as Bangladesh. However, prospective population-specific data identifying short-term prognostic factors are limited. This study aimed to examine the clinical, radiological, and in-hospital factors associated with 30-day functional outcome and early mortality in a selected two-center cohort of Bangladeshi patients with spontaneous intracerebral hemorrhage. Methods This prospective cohort study was conducted in two tertiary referral centers in Dhaka between February 2021 and January 2023. Adult patients with first-ever spontaneous intracerebral hemorrhage confirmed by computed tomography and presenting within 72 hours were enrolled. Eligibility was restricted to patients with a baseline NIHSS of 5-15, defining a selected, moderate-severity cohort. Baseline demographic, clinical, laboratory, and radiological variables were recorded. Functional outcome at 30 days was assessed using the modified Rankin Scale. Unfavorable functional outcome (mRS 4-6, which includes death) was the primary outcome, and 30-day mortality was a secondary outcome. Multivariable logistic regression was used to examine factors associated with unfavorable outcomes, and Cox proportional hazards models were applied to examine factors associated with 30-day mortality. Results Among 220 patients, 72 (32.7%) died within 30 days, and 130 (59.1%) had unfavorable outcomes at 30 days. Overall, 90 (40.9%) patients had a favorable outcome (mRS 0-3) and 130 (59.1%) had an unfavorable outcome (mRS 4-6), the latter including the 72 deaths. Increasing age was independently associated with poor functional outcome (adjusted OR 1.07 per year; 95% CI 1.04-1.11; p < 0.001). Hemiparesis at admission (OR 7.05; 95% CI 1.65-30.11; p = 0.008), aspiration pneumonia (OR 4.63; 95% CI 1.64-13.10; p = 0.004), and hypernatremia (OR 14.34; 95% CI 2.26-91.16; p = 0.005) were also associated with unfavourable outcome, although aspiration pneumonia and hypernatremia are post-admission complications rather than baseline predictors. For mortality, older age (adjusted HR 1.02; 95% CI 1.00-1.04; p = 0.029) and higher baseline NIHSS (HR 1.23; 95% CI 1.09-1.39; p = 0.001) were independently associated with death, whereas the in-hospital complications aspiration pneumonia (HR 3.34; 95% CI 1.94-5.74; p < 0.001) and hypernatremia (HR 3.30; 95% CI 1.99-5.82; p < 0.001) were associated with higher mortality but, as time-dependent events, should not be interpreted as baseline predictors. Conclusion Advancing age, greater neurological severity, and in-hospital complications such as aspiration pneumonia and hypernatremia were associated with short-term functional outcome and mortality. These associations may help identify high-risk patients, but because this was an observational study of a selected cohort in which in-hospital complications were analyzed as fixed covariates, the findings should not be interpreted as evidence that management of these complications improves outcomes.

title: Variability in Bracing Design and Bracing Protocols for the Non-Operative Management of Legg-Calvé-Perthes Disease: A Scoping Systematic Review.
abstract: Legg-Calvé-Perthes disease (LCPD) is a self-limiting avascular necrosis of the femoral head in children, with management aimed at preserving hip joint congruency and reducing the risk of long-term degenerative changes. Bracing is a commonly used containment strategy; however, its effectiveness remains controversial owing to variation in brace design, biomechanical principles, and treatment protocols. This systematic review evaluates and synthesizes the variability in bracing design and bracing protocols for non-operative management of LCPD. This review adhered to the PRISMA-ScR guidelines. A comprehensive search of PubMed, Scopus, Science Citation Index, and Google Scholar was performed using keywords such as "Perthes" OR "Coxa Plana" and "treatment" OR "non-operative" OR "orthoses" OR "conservative" OR "brace". Only full-text articles in English were included. Studies were required to document initial radiographs using the Catterall or Herring classification and assess outcomes with the Mose or Stulberg criteria. Exclusion criteria included non-English language articles and research with inadequate methodology. Patient demographics, therapy type, type of bracing, and radiological results were among the information retrieved. Radiographic results were classified as good or poor using the Mose and Stulberg ratings. A total of 12 studies were examined to determine the efficacy of conservative treatments, especially bracing, for LCPD. Age of onset was a key prognostic factor, with better outcomes indicated in children under the age of eight. Bracing was more beneficial in younger individuals with milder illness, although adherence was crucial. Various braces, including the Atlanta Scottish Rite, trilateral socket, and non-weight-bearing ambulatory hip abduction brace, have been developed to maintain hip abduction. However, limitations such as discomfort, poor adherence, reduced mobility, and inconsistent radiological and clinical outcomes undermine their efficacy. Additionally, significant variability exists in indications, duration, and patient selection, with no universally accepted bracing protocol. Despite theoretical containment advantages, the effectiveness of bracing in LCPD remains inconclusive due to heterogeneity in brace designs, patient selection, and treatment protocols, as well as limitations in the underlying evidence base. Further prospective, methodologically robust studies with standardized protocols and transparent reporting of adherence are needed to clarify the role of bracing in clinically meaningful outcomes.

title: Papillary Tumor of the Pineal Region Presenting With Obstructive Hydrocephalus: A Diagnostic and Management Challenge.
abstract: We report a 45-year-old woman with a papillary tumor of the pineal region (PTPR), a neuroepithelial neoplasm of the pineal gland, who presented with a one-year history of headaches, visual disturbance, and gait impairment and was found to have a pineal mass with obstructive hydrocephalus. She underwent endoscopic third ventriculostomy (ETV) with biopsy; the initial radiologic impression favored pineocytoma. Immunohistochemistry was nondiagnostic on the limited sample, and the diagnosis of PTPR was established only after review at two academic neuropathology centers. DNA methylation profiling was obtained for definitive molecular classification, with the result not yet available for review at the time of reporting. The lesion was resected via an interhemispheric transcallosal approach, but the patient developed recurrent hydrocephalus due to ETV failure, requiring a ventriculoperitoneal shunt. She completed adjuvant radiotherapy and showed no recurrence on the most recent surveillance MRI. In this patient, PTPR posed two challenges: diagnostic overlap with pineocytoma that required specialized and molecular workup, and persistent hydrocephalus after ETV failure that ultimately required permanent cerebrospinal fluid diversion.

title: Atypical Lyme Neuroborreliosis Presenting With Ventriculitis and Cerebritis: A Case Report.
abstract: Lyme neuroborreliosis is a neurological manifestation of infection by Borrelia burgdorferi sensu lato and most commonly presents with lymphocytic meningitis, cranial neuropathy, or painful radiculitis. Central nervous system parenchymal involvement is uncommon, and ventriculitis is rarely reported. We describe a man in his late 70s who presented with acute confusion, dysarthria, and left-sided weakness following several days of severe lower-limb pain and progressive mobility impairment. His neurological status rapidly deteriorated, with secondary seizures requiring invasive mechanical ventilation and intensive care support. Laboratory evaluation demonstrated a marked systemic inflammatory response, thrombocytopenia, acute kidney injury, and cholestatic liver dysfunction. Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) analysis revealed pleocytosis with initial neutrophilic predominance, markedly elevated protein, and preserved glucose. Routine bacterial cultures and molecular testing for common central nervous system pathogens were negative. Anti- Borrelia IgG and IgM antibodies were detected in CSF, although a paired CSF-serum antibody index was unavailable. Brain magnetic resonance imaging demonstrated inflammatory material within the occipital horns of the lateral ventricles, bilateral leptomeningeal involvement, and focal parenchymal lesions with restricted diffusion suggestive of cerebritis. In the appropriate clinical context, these findings supported a diagnosis of probable Lyme neuroborreliosis with an unusual ventriculitis-like presentation. Despite prolonged antimicrobial therapy and partial improvement in CSF and radiological inflammatory findings, neurological recovery remained limited, and the patient subsequently died following ventilator-associated pneumonia complicated by septic shock. This case illustrates an uncommon and severe central nervous system presentation potentially associated with Lyme neuroborreliosis and highlights both the diagnostic value and limitations of CSF serology when demonstration of intrathecal antibody synthesis is unavailable.

title: Relative Brain Perfusion Differences in a Patient With Persistent Cognitive Symptoms: A Case Report.
abstract: Persistent cognitive symptoms in older adults may occur in the setting of multiple overlapping neurologic, vascular, sleep-related, psychiatric, and medical factors. We report the case of a 69-year-old man with several years of progressive short-term memory difficulty, cognitive slowing, word-finding difficulty, reduced decisiveness, and collateral concern regarding gait change. The clinical evaluation identified several potentially relevant contributors, including persistent dyslipidemia, inadequately treated obstructive sleep apnea, mild depressive symptoms, and a reported prior cerebrovascular finding. Portions of the outside diagnostic evaluation were unavailable for independent review. Brain perfusion single-photon emission computed tomography (SPECT), obtained as an adjunctive component of the clinical evaluation, demonstrated a nonspecific mixed pattern of relative cortical and subcortical tracer-distribution differences. An individualized management plan was subsequently implemented, focusing on potentially modifiable contributors, sleep optimization, lifestyle measures, and depressive symptoms. At approximately three-month follow-up, the patient's spouse reported no significant memory improvement but no noticeable decline; subsequent follow-up raised renewed concern regarding progression. Because repeat standardized cognitive testing was not performed and multiple interventions were introduced over time, the longitudinal clinical course could not be objectively quantified or attributed to any individual intervention. This case describes a nonspecific pattern of relative brain perfusion differences in a patient with persistent cognitive symptoms. The relationship between these imaging findings and the patient's clinical symptoms remains uncertain, and this single observation does not establish a specific neurologic etiology or the diagnostic, prognostic, or treatment-selection utility of brain perfusion SPECT.

title: A Rare Case of Large Cell Neuroendocrine Carcinoma of the Thymus Presenting as a Lower Neck Mass in a Young Male Patient.
abstract: Large cell neuroendocrine carcinoma (LCNEC) of the thymus is a strikingly unusual and high-grade thymic tumor with a poor prognosis. Studies with large series of patients on the clinical, epidemiological, and biological behavior of the disease are not available due to its low prevalence and short survival. We report here such a rare case of LCNEC in a 33-year-old male patient who primarily presented with a mass in the suprasternal and left supraclavicular regions with multiple bilateral cervical lymph nodes. Fine needle aspiration cytology from the neck mass demonstrated hypercellular smears with numerous variably sized, loosely cohesive clusters, including large hypercellular ones, of medium-sized atypical cells with scant cytoplasm, hyperchromatic nuclei, and granular chromatin, with a few having small, inconspicuous nucleoli. Peripheral nuclear palisading or rosette-like structures were noted in many places. An anterior mediastinal invasive mass lesion, possibly of thymic origin, extending to the neck and encasing the major vessels, including branches of the aortic arch, without any evidence of lung parenchymal extension, with multiple bilateral cervical lymph nodes was identified on contrast-enhanced computed tomography. Incisional biopsy revealed large atypical cells mostly arranged in nests, solid sheets, and trabeculae, with hyperchromatic nuclei, coarse chromatin, a moderate amount of eosinophilic cytoplasm, frequent mitoses, and apoptotic bodies. The cells were immunopositive for pancytokeratin, EMA, synaptophysin, chromogranin A, CD56, and TTF-1, with a high Ki-67 labeling index, while negative for all other relevant markers. Misdiagnosis or delay in the correct diagnosis of this rare but aggressive thymic tumor may lead to disease spread and progression to systemic involvement. Many such cases of thymic LCNEC need to be studied to design and optimize standard management.

Many such cases of thymic LCNEC need to be studied to design and optimize standard management.

title: Bilateral Painless Vision Loss From Probable Leptomeningeal Metastasis During Systemic Response in Esophageal Adenocarcinoma.
abstract: Leptomeningeal metastasis (LM) is a rare complication of esophageal adenocarcinoma, with reported cases typically presenting with meningitic, encephalopathic, or multifocal neurologic symptoms. We report a 70-year-old man with metastatic esophageal adenocarcinoma with signet-ring cell features who developed subacute, painless, bilateral visual loss with bilateral optic disc edema as the initial manifestation of probable LM. Symptoms arose four months into first-line folinic acid, fluorouracil, and oxaliplatin (FOLFOX) plus pembrolizumab while all measurable extracranial disease was responding and in the absence of headache, meningismus, or other neurologic symptoms. Contrast-enhanced MRI demonstrated bilateral optic nerve sheath enhancement with subtle linear leptomeningeal enhancement over the cerebral convexities and no parenchymal brain metastases. Over the ensuing days, the patient developed urinary incontinence, gait instability, lower-extremity weakness, and cognitive decline. Cerebrospinal fluid analysis showed markedly elevated protein, lymphocytic pleocytosis, normal glucose, and rare atypical cells suspicious for malignancy; flow cytometry and cultures were negative. Although CSF cytology was not definitively diagnostic, the combined clinical presentation, characteristic MRI findings, and supportive CSF abnormalities in the setting of known metastatic malignancy were consistent with probable LM. Whole-brain radiotherapy was initiated but discontinued after one fraction because of rapid neurologic deterioration, and the patient died four weeks after the diagnosis. This case highlights an unusual presentation of probable LM in esophageal adenocarcinoma, with subacute painless bilateral visual loss and optic disc edema preceding other neurologic manifestations despite concurrent extracranial disease response.

title: Skin Metastasis of an Occult Primary Bronchopulmonary Disease: A Case Report and Literature Review.
abstract: Cutaneous metastases of pulmonary origin are rare but clinically significant, typically indicating advanced disease with a poor prognosis. They may occasionally reveal an occult lung cancer, as illustrated by the case reported here. We report the case of a 78-year-old man, a former heavy smoker, who presented with a rapidly growing, ulcerated, exophytic nodule on the anterior chest wall. Skin biopsy revealed a poorly differentiated adenocarcinoma, with negative thyroid transcription factor-1 (TTF-1) and Napsin A staining, raising diagnostic difficulty regarding the primary origin. Chest CT subsequently identified a 4.1 cm tumor of the right lower lobe, and bronchoscopic biopsy confirmed a bronchial adenocarcinoma. Staging revealed disseminated disease (cT2b cN1 cM1c, Stage IVB) with cerebral, adrenal, and bone metastases. A multidisciplinary tumor board recommended whole-brain radiotherapy (30 Gy in 10 fractions) combined with palliative chemotherapy (cisplatin-gemcitabine), with stable disease observed at six months of follow-up. This case underlines the limitations of TTF-1 and Napsin A negativity in excluding a pulmonary origin, particularly in poorly differentiated tumors, and highlights the value of an integrated clinical, radiological, morphological, and immunohistochemical approach. Management of extensively disseminated disease remains essentially palliative; surgery has no impact on survival and is reserved for palliative or diagnostic indications.

title: Masquerade Syndrome Presenting as Optic Neuritis and Retinitis Due to Pituitary Germinoma.
abstract: Masquerade syndrome is a collective term for various ocular diseases presenting with clinical features resembling intraocular inflammation. Delays in definitive diagnosis and treatment can not only lead to irreversible vision loss but also impact the patient's prognosis regarding survival. We report the case of a 26-year-old male patient who presented with impaired vision in the right eye, which had persisted for six months; neuroretinitis was diagnosed. Although infectious neuroretinitis was suspected, tests for pathogens such as Mycobacterium tuberculosis , Toxoplasma , Toxocara , and Bartonella were all negative. Treatment with betamethasone eye drops alone resulted in a fluctuating course of improvement and worsening of the neuroretinitis. Ten months after the initial visit, the patient's headache-which had begun one month prior-worsened and was accompanied by vomiting and a pulsating sensation, leading to a consultation with our department of neurosurgery. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) revealed a lobulated mass extending from the right midbrain to the right thalamus, causing narrowing of the cerebral aqueduct and hydrocephalus. Four days after the neurosurgical consultation, the patient underwent endoscopic third ventriculostomy (ETV) and a brain biopsy, leading to a definitive diagnosis of germinoma. The headache improved the day after surgery, and by one month after the operation, the hydrocephalus had resolved, while neuroretinitis also showed improvement. The patient received carboplatin and etoposide (CARE) treatment in the second, third, and fourth months post-surgery, whole-ventricle radiotherapy (24 Gy/15 fractions) in the fifth and sixth months, and ifosfamide (IFO), cisplatin (CDDP), and etoposide (VP-16) (ICE) treatment in the seventh, ninth, and 11th months. No recurrence of the brain tumor has been observed since then. At the final follow-up visit five years post-surgery, the neuroretinitis had resolved. When neuroretinitis is observed in a young patient and infectious causes have been ruled out, intracranial germinoma should be considered in the differential diagnosis.
